headings: 5.6 THE WORK-ENERGY THEOREM FOR A VARIABLE FORCE
pages.page_summary: This page concludes the discussion on work done by a variable force using graphical representation (Fig. 5.3) and provides a worked example (Example 5.5) involving a woman pushing a trunk. It then derives the Work-Energy Theorem for a variable force in one dimension, showing that the change in kinetic energy equals the integral of force over displacement.
knowledge_points: The work done by a variable force is equal to the area under the force-displacement curve.
Example 5.5: A woman applies a force of 100 N for 10 m, then the force reduces linearly to 50 N over the next 10 m (total 20 m). The frictional force is constant at 50 N.
The work done by the applied force is calculated as the area of a rectangle (100 N * 10 m) plus the area of a trapezium (average of 100 N and 50 N * 10 m), totaling 1750 J.
The work done by the frictional force is negative because it opposes motion, calculated as -50 N * 20 m = -1000 J.
The Work-Energy Theorem for a variable force is derived by integrating Newton's Second Law (F = ma) with respect to displacement.
The theorem states that the change in kinetic energy (Kf - Ki) is equal to the work done (W) or the integral of force over displacement.

visuals.description: Fig. 5.4 is a graph plotting the applied force F (blue line) and the opposing frictional force f (dashed line) against displacement x. The applied force is constant at 100 N from 0 to 10 m, then decreases linearly to 50 N at 20 m. The frictional force is constant at -50 N. The areas under the curves are marked with points A, B, C, D, E, G, H, I.
visuals.educational_role: Visualizes the specific force profile for Example 5.5, allowing the calculation of work as the area of geometric shapes (rectangle and trapezium).
